title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Western Michigan utilities brace for AI power demand; will rates and reliability hold?

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's a sunny Sunday morning here in August, and we're diving into fresh questions from Mason County about whether the local grid can keep up with proposed AI data centers.
That Mason County story from Friday really highlights the bigger tension playing out across the state right now.
Exactly. Western Michigan utilities are staring down rising demand from these facilities, and residents want to know if new power plants or upgrades are coming — and crucially, who foots the bill.
So walk me through the history here, Graham. How did we get to this point where one county is suddenly asking these questions?

Well, data centers have been circling Michigan for a while now, drawn by cheap land and cooling potential. But the scale of AI projects is new — we're talking loads that can rival small cities in power use.
And that strain on transmission lines sounds serious. What happens if the grid can't handle it?

Blackouts become a real risk for homes and factories, and any upgrades mean higher rates passed along to regular customers. Mason County folks are rightly asking if these projects can even locate there without those downsides.
Who are the main players pushing these proposals in western Michigan?
Local utilities are fielding the inquiries, along with developers eyeing sites for AI campuses. Regulators at the state level are also in the mix now.
And what about the water angle? These places need massive cooling, right?
They do, and that ties into farmland and town impacts too. Drawing that much water and power can affect everything from local agriculture to everyday utility costs.
How does this compare to fights we've seen elsewhere in the state?
It's the same pattern — communities weighing jobs and investment against reliability, bills, and quality of life. Mason County is just the latest spot voicing those concerns out loud.
What do you think happens next? Will we see new plants built, or more upgrades funded by ratepayers?
That's the open question. Regulators will have to decide how to handle these big new loads, and local input like we're hearing from Mason County will shape that.
I'm curious about the emissions and noise side too if on-site power comes into play.
Those are fresh concerns that come with any workaround to grid delays. It could speed things up but raises other issues for nearby residents.
And for towns 30 or 60 miles away — why should they care about Mason County specifically?
Because utility rates are regional. If upgrades get approved there, costs can ripple out to other DTE or Consumers Energy customers across western and even parts of southeast Michigan.
Got it. So this isn't just a local Mason story — it's a statewide signal.
Precisely. The conversation is shifting from whether data centers come to how we manage the infrastructure they need.
What would stronger oversight look like here?
Maybe requirements that developers pay for upgrades upfront, or limits on project size until the grid catches up. Residents are pushing for that kind of accountability.
And if nothing changes, what are the stakes for everyday folks?
Higher bills, potential reliability issues, and lost farmland or quiet nights in rural areas. It's a lot to weigh.
Thanks for laying that out. Let's move to some other developments from this week.
Sure. Starting with Attorney General Dana Nessel on Friday pressing the Public Service Commission for answers on how it's handling these surging power demands.
Why is she getting involved now?
She's concerned residents could see higher bills if large loads get approved without enough checks. It signals pushback at the state level.
Moving on, OpenAI offered help Friday after that water system hack linked to data center growth pressures.
Right — cybersecurity on utilities supplying cooling is suddenly a bigger priority. Any new cluster will depend on those same systems.
A Michigan firm pitched on-site power Friday to bypass grid delays for AI campuses.
That approach could accelerate projects but brings up emissions, noise, and payment questions when the grid is already tight.
Detroit released a new assessment Friday showing data centers could add hundreds of megawatts on a strained grid.
City planners are drafting rules with size limits and requirements that developers cover upgrades — and suburban DTE customers could feel the rate impact too.
Over in Cass County, Thursday brought complaints about nonstop noise from an existing facility in Dowagiac.
Residents describe constant sound with no quick fix from officials. It's a reminder of the quality-of-life side that lingers after projects are built.
Pittsfield Township is tightening zoning Thursday after resident concerns over noise, traffic, and power near Ann Arbor.
Those changes could become a model for other Washtenaw County townships and help protect against sprawl.
Wednesday, Monroe Township asked a federal judge to dismiss a $300 million lawsuit over its data center ban.
The case tests whether locals can block big power and water draws. Southeast Michigan residents have a stake in the outcome.
Also Wednesday, a data center opponent won a Democratic primary for state House.
That win moves the debate into the legislature for that district and shows voter sentiment shifting.
And Washtenaw voters rejected a $1 billion rezoning Wednesday in a rural township near Ann Arbor.
The decision protects farmland and infrastructure from heavy power and water use.
Quite a week of local pushback and regulatory questions.
Now for On Deck — no major public meetings listed for today specifically, but several township boards across the state are expected to discuss zoning and grid issues this week.
Listeners should check their local calendars for any updates on those.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Mason County Grid Faces AI Data Center Surge — Who Pays for Upgrades?
